Surgical Breast Enlargement

Preparing for Revision Surgery: Records, Questions and Expectations

Revision surgery requires more preparation than a first operation. Good records and a clear diagnosis make planning safer.

Home/Surgical Breast Enlargement/Breast revision/Preparing for Revision Surgery: Records, Questions and Expectations

Revision surgery requires more preparation than a first operation. Good records, a clear diagnosis and realistic expectations make planning safer.

Gather your records

  • Implant card with manufacturer, model, size and batch
  • Operation notes and details from your first surgery
  • Imaging reports such as ultrasound, MRI or mammograms
  • Photos from before and after your first operation
  • Medical history and medications

If you cannot find them, ask the original clinic or hospital for copies.

Get a clear diagnosis

Ask what is wrong and what evidence supports it. Imaging may be needed to check for rupture, fluid or capsule changes.

Consider a second opinion

A different surgeon may suggest a different approach. This is reasonable and common, especially for complex revision.

Set realistic expectations

  • Revision may be less predictable than first-time surgery
  • Risks of complications can be higher
  • Results may not match what you originally had or wanted
  • More than one operation may be needed

Practical matters

Ask about costs, whether implants will be replaced, warranty coverage and recovery time. Check what the original surgeon or clinic offers, if anything, for complications. Get a written estimate before proceeding.

Optimise health before surgery

Revision planning should include a review of smoking or nicotine exposure, medicines and supplements, blood-clot risk, diabetes control and any previous healing problems. Your surgeon or anaesthetist may ask for tests or recommend delaying surgery until a modifiable risk is addressed. Do not stop prescribed medicines without medical advice.

Plan around uncertainty

Scar tissue and implant findings can be clearer during surgery than on a scan. Ask which decisions are fixed, which might change in theatre and who will discuss an unexpected result with you. A written plan can make choices about replacement, removal and pathology easier to revisit calmly.

Prepare practical support

Arrange a responsible adult, time away from work and help with lifting, children or household tasks if needed. Confirm the contact route for after-hours concerns and the schedule for wound checks. Practical preparation reduces pressure to resume activity before your surgical team says it is safe.

Emotional side

Revision can feel frustrating or distressing. Support from friends, family or a counsellor can help.

Questions to ask

  • How many revisions like mine have you done?
  • What is the goal, and what is a realistic result?
  • What risks apply to me specifically?
  • What if the result is not what I hoped?

Key takeaway

Good records and a clear plan make revision safer and less stressful. See Breast Revision Surgery.
